newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: DE KLERK URGES S.AFRICAN PARTIES TO COOPERATE.
newsitem.headline: DE KLERK URGES S.AFRICAN PARTIES TO COOPERATE.

text.p: South Africa's former president F.W. De Klerk called on Thursday for closer cooperation between parties opposing Nelson Mandela's government, but stopped short of urging them to form an alliance.
"We want to dispel the perception which has been created that the National Party (NP) is seeking an alliance or alliances with any party," he told a news conference.

"Our agenda is to lay a foundation for closer and maybe even a structured cooperation in respect of issues where opposition parties share the same concerns and promote the same solutions." South African media have speculated that the NP, which until the middle of last year was a junior partner in Mandela's unity government, was seeking to form an opposition alliance with other rivals of the ruling African National Congress.
NP leaders say they are looking at the possibility of a vaguer movement grouping parties and non-political organisations which share their free-market values.
The NP has in recent months had talks with the leader of the Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP), Mangosuthu Buthelezi, and of the Democratic Party, Tony Leon.
De Klerk said the NP would also be meeting with leaders of other parliamentary parties.
Political analysts have in the past suggested that the NP's call for closer links, especially with black dominated parties, could be an attempt to boost its poor support in black areas.
NP leaders acknowledge that they will never have a chance of regaining power unless they break out of their narrow historical support base among white South Africans.
In South Africa's first all-race elections in 1994, the NP won 40 out of 400 seats in the national assembly. It also won control of only one of the country's nine provinces.
De Klerk, speaking a day before the opening of parliament, said the envisaged cooperation would not sign away any party's right to differ on issues.
"All this (cooperation) should take place on the basis of not undermining the autonomy or identity of any party," he said.
